chapters.name: Introduction
chapters.intro:
The first step is to restrict Black's King to one of the green triangles we see on the board in this position. We will control the long diagonal of the triangle with our Bishop, and we will control the necessary dark squares using our Knight and King.

Move your King closer to the center to read about step 2 in the overall plan. [%csl Ga8,Gh1][%cal Gb1h7,Gh7h1,Ga2g8,Gg8a8,Be1e2,Ga2a8,Gb1h1]

studies.study_name: 7th-Rank Rook Pawn with a Passive Rook

chapters.name: King on f7
chapters.intro: Since the Black king is not on one of the red squares, we know this is a win for White. Let's win this game by playing the only winning move . [%csl Rg7,Rh7,Rb7,Rc7,Rb6,Rc6,Ra6,Ra2,Ra1][%cal Ga8h8]

chapters.name: King on g7
chapters.intro:
To draw this position as Black we keep our King on g7 or h7, and we keep our Rook on the promotion file whenever we can. If White moves their King next to their pawn we have to check it away.

Right now, White isn't threatening anything, so we can just shuffle our King between g7 and h7. [%csl Rh7,Rg7,Rc7,Rb7,Rc6,Rb6,Ra6,Ra2,Ra1][%cal Gg7h7]

chapters.name: King on g7, extra g-pawn
chapters.intro: An extra pawn on g3 has been introduced. What difference does it make? Well, if we push it to g6, it takes away the h7 square from Black's King. [%csl Rg7,Rh7,Ra2,Ra1,Rb7,Rc7,Rc6,Rb6,Ra6][%cal Gg3g4]

chapters.name: King on g7, extra b-f pawn
chapters.intro: An extra g-pawn does not help White, but an extra b-, c-, d-, e-, or f-pawn does win for White. Why? Because we can now force Black's King away from g7 and h7. [%csl Gf2,Ge2,Gd2,Gc2,Gb2][%cal Gf3f4]

chapters.name: Put Your Opponent's Cart Before their Horse
Rook vs Pawn: Cutting off the King
Rook vs Pawn Draw
chapters.intro: [%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] In this interesting position, the main idea for black to be able to draw is to not obstruct the pawn on the a-file and be cut off by white's rook. Thus black always needs to put their king on the c-file if white check them with the rook on the b-file.

chapters.name: Vancura Position
chapters.intro:
[%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] The Vančura position is not a very common ending. It was studied by Josef Vančura and his analysis was published in 1924. The key idea is to keep giving lateral checks to drive White's king away from the queenside until white pushes the pawn to a7, then to play Ra6 to reach another well-known drawn rook ending.

Note that in the Vančura position, we can't try to do checks from the 1st rank because white's king can hide on a7 and then white will be able to promote the pawn with the help of the rook.

In this position, we can start the sequence of checks with Rf5.

chapters.name: Frontal Defense
chapters.intro:
[%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] A frontal defense is best used when the pawn has not advanced to the 5th rank. Despite the Black king being two files away from the passed pawn, the game is still salvageable. Black survives by giving a barrage of checks, preventing the white king from making progress.

First, we need to prevent white from playing b5 right away.

chapters.name: When the Frontal Defense doesn't work
When the Back Rank Defense doesn't work
Rook and Rook Pawn versus Rook
Holding Against a Rook Pawn
chapters.intro:
[%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] For rook endings with a rook pawn, as long as the king is 3 files away from the enemy pawn the ending is holdable because Black's king can make it in time to the crucial c7 square when white tries to bring the rook to the b-file to make a bridge. It is important to keep white's king obstructing the pawn with our rook on the b-file.

Move the rook to b3 to continue the exercise. [%csl Gc7][%cal Gb1b3]

chapters.name: Advanced Philidor
chapters.intro: [%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] At first, this might look lost, as 1...Rg5 loses immediately to 2.Kd6. However, there is a way to hold this, with the Philidor idea of using the rook from behind. Bring the rook to f2 to continue the exercise. [%cal Gf5f2]

chapters.name: A Position From Dvoretsky
chapters.intro:
[%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] We covered all the Rook and Pawn vs Rook positions, the next 4 chapters are about a rook vs one or more pawns.

This position comes from Dvoretsky's endgames manual. The idea is to bring the king in a way that black's promotion to a queen doesn't come with a check, so white can checkmate black with the rook.

chapters.name: Rook versus Two Pawns
chapters.intro: [%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] The key idea is to park the king on h7 and advance the g-pawn. If we try to advance the h-pawn we will actually be too slow.

chapters.name: A study by Saavedra
chapters.intro: [%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] This is a very well-known study named after Fernando Saavedra. Try to solve it!

chapters.name: A Tricky Resource
chapters.intro: [%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] At first glance, it looks like White may have lost this game, as Black's pawns have made it all the way to the 6th rank. However, there is one last drawing trick.

chapters.name: R2p vs R - Stalemate Trick
chapters.intro: [%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] Currently, black isn't threatening anything, so we can play a waiting move. Play Ra3 to continue the exercise. [%cal Gb3a3]

chapters.name: Kasparian's Draw
chapters.intro:
[%anno "Yeltcki", yeltcki] There are some special cases where rook +2 connected passers vs rook is drawn. Here is one of them.

Here, all what black needs to do is bring the king to help the pawns and the rook, but we can't cut off the king right away since h3 would be winning for black. Therefore white needs to create a threat first.
